A subsequent large randomised study also found that pre-operative chemoradiotherapy (fluorouracil infusion plus fractionated pelvic radiotherapy) improved local control and was associated with less toxicity than postoperative treatment, but did not improve overall sur- vival.18 US guidelines recommend pre-operative chemoradiother- apy with fluorouracil, alone or with folinic acid, as the chemotherapy component in most patients with stage II or III disease;5 it is suggested that oral capecitabine may be a valid alternative to fluorouracil. After surgery, adjuvant chemotherapy with a fluorouracil regimen, FOLFOX, or capecitabine is recommended, although the latter 2 options are extrapolations from results in colon cancer; a com- bined chemoradiotherapy regimen may be used in some patients. Palliative treatments for advanced colorectal cancer (stage IV; metastatic disease) include surgery, radiothera- py, and chemotherapy.1,2,4,5,10,19,20 Metastasis usually oc- curs first to the liver: about 20 to 25% of patients have de- tectable liver metastases at initial diagnosis in the UK, and a further 40 to 50% develop metastases within 3 years of primary surgery. Somewhat under 10% of these cases are localised and resectable,19 and surgery offers a chance of prolonged survival.2,19 Systemic neoadjuvant chemothera- py can reduce tumour volume and render some previously unresectable metastases suitable candidates for surgery.2,4 Another potential approach is the adjuvant use of intrapor- tal chemotherapy directed at the liver. In a meta-analysis of 10 studies,21 the reduction in hepatic metastases with in- traportal vein chemotherapy given for about 1 week after surgery was not significant, although there was a trend to- wards increased 5-year survival. It was concluded that ad- ditional trial evidence was required.21 Conventional palliative chemotherapy is based on the use of fluorouracil, and has been shown to produce modest survival benefits.22 Adding folinic acid improves the effi- cacy,23 and the combination has long been regarded as standard.
